label: Network curvature appears in node counts via the Ricci scalar
statement: In a large network approximating d-dimensional space, the leading correction to the number of nodes reached within distance r is proportional to the Ricci scalar curvature times r^(d+1), so curvature can be determined purely from network connectivity.
quote: But in fact the leading correction to the number of nodes reached is always quite simple: it is just proportional to what is called the Ricci scalar curvature, multiplied by rd + 1.
scope: large networks approximating curved Riemannian spaces

label: Causal invariant dimension-preserving network rules give Einstein equations
statement: Network replacement rules that are causal invariant and maintain a fixed number of dimensions will almost inevitably produce large-scale behavior close to the vacuum Einstein equations of general relativity, analogous to how Navier–Stokes behavior emerges from cellular automaton fluids.
quote: But I suspect that if one has replacement rules that are causal invariant and that in effect successfully maintain a fixed number of dimensions they will almost inevitably lead to behavior that follows something close to the Einstein equations.
scope: causal invariant network rewriting systems and general relativity

label: Network-based programs will reproduce the key features of quantum theory
statement: Discrete network models of the universe with causal invariance will ultimately turn out to exhibit many if not all of the key features of quantum theory, even though they are not set up in terms of its standard formalism.
quote: And in fact it is my strong suspicion that the kinds of programs that I have discussed in the past few sections will actually in the end turn out to show many if not all the key features of quantum theory.
scope: network models of the universe and quantum phenomena

label: Network threads let deterministic models produce quantum correlations
statement: The quantum correlations between distant particles usually taken to rule out definite underlying processes can arise in a deterministic network model, because particles created together stay linked by threads of connections that bypass ordinary three-dimensional space.
quote: And the basic reason for this is that if the universe is a network then it can in a sense easily contain threads that continue to connect particles even when the particles get far apart in terms of ordinary space.
scope: correlations in measurements on entangled particle pairs (Bell-type experiments)

label: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs
statement: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
quote: the evidence we have suggests that the basic mechanisms at work can once again successfully be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
scope: human perception and methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis

label: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard
statement: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.
quote: But for the more general rules that I discuss in this book it appears to often be extremely difficult. For even though the rules may be simple, the behavior they produce is often highly complex, and shows absolutely no obvious trace of its simple origins.
scope: inference of generating rules from the output of cellular automata and other simple programs

label: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions
statement: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.
quote: Indeed, what I suspect is that ultimately no useful definition of randomness can be based solely on the issue of what short descriptions of something may in principle exist.
scope: definitions of randomness, including description-length (algorithmic) definitions

label: Something is random if essentially no simple program detects regularities in it
statement: Since essentially all standard methods of perception and analysis are based on simple programs, something should be considered random whenever essentially no simple program succeeds in detecting regularities in it.
quote: something should be considered to be random whenever there is essentially no simple program that can succeed in detecting regularities in it.
scope: the definition of randomness for data of any kind

label: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do
statement: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.
quote: For once a few simple programs corresponding to a few standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed in detecting them.
scope: detection of regularities in sequences and images by simple programs

label: Complexity means our perception and analysis fail to find a short description
statement: To call something complex is to say that our methods of perception and analysis have failed to find a short description of the features of it that we are interested in; complexity therefore depends on which features one chooses to capture.
quote: when we say that something seems complex, what we are effectively saying is that our powers of perception and analysis have failed on it.
scope: the definition of complexity

label: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features
statement: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.
quote: the images that draw us in the most—and typically that we find the most aesthetically pleasing—are those for which some features are simple for us to describe, but others have no short description that can be found by any of our standard processes of visual perception.
scope: human visual attention and aesthetic preference for images

label: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else
statement: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior even when it is generated by very short programs.
quote: Essentially every method, for example, will successfully compress large regions of uniform color. And most methods manage to compress behavior that is repetitive, and at least to some extent behavior that is nested—exactly the two kinds of simple behavior that we have noted many times in this book.
scope: lossless data compression algorithms applied to patterns from simple programs

label: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression
statement: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this substantially.
quote: But images that one would normally consider complex tend to have features that cannot be recognized except at significantly lower levels of compression.
scope: lossy transform-based image compression of simple, random and complex images

label: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features
statement: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.
quote: I strongly suspect that it is density differences such as these that allow our visual system to distinguish textures.
scope: human visual texture perception

label: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting
statement: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.
quote: it is remarkably difficult for us to tell that the patterns are nested. And this can be viewed as a clear example of a limitation in our powers of visual perception.
scope: human visual recognition of repetitive and nested two-dimensional patterns

label: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else
statement: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.
quote: we readily recognize exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies, and essentially nothing else.
scope: human auditory perception of sounds generated from discrete sequences

label: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data
statement: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.
quote: In most cases, the typical behavior produced by the model looks considerably more random than the data.
scope: statistical modeling of data generated by deterministic simple programs

label: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test
statement: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small spread of those frequencies.
quote: it has sometimes been thought that if one could just compute frequencies of blocks of all lengths one would have a kind of universal test for randomness. But sequences like (e) and (f) on the facing page make it clear that this is not the case.
scope: block-frequency tests for randomness of binary sequences

label: Rule 30 center column and digits of pi pass statistical tests for randomness
statement: The center column of the rule 30 cellular automaton and the base 2 digits of pi show no detectable deviation from randomness under block-frequency statistics or under analysis by simple cellular automata, even though both are generated by simple rules.
quote: statistical analysis, even with some generalization, cannot readily recognize that sequences like (g) and (h) are anything but completely random—even though at an underlying level these sequences were generated by quite simple rules.
scope: the rule 30 center-column sequence and the binary expansion of pi

label: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known
statement: Simple rules with complex behavior, such as the rule 30 cellular automaton sampled sparsely to give an encrypting sequence, can be used to build stream ciphers at least as secure against cryptanalysis as any known system, unlike additive cellular automata or linear feedback shift registers, whose keys are easily recovered.
quote: I strongly suspect that they can, and that in fact they allow one to construct systems that are at least as secure to cryptanalysis as any that are known.
scope: stream ciphers based on cellular automata, specifically rule 30

label: Every nested pattern likely has a formula in generalized hypergeometric functions
statement: Although most nested patterns have no obvious relation to ordinary mathematical functions, a formula for the color of each cell of any nested pattern can probably be found in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions or similar generalizations of traditional functions.
quote: it is my guess that in the end it will in fact turn out to be possible to get a formula for any nested pattern in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions
scope: nested patterns generated by substitution systems

label: No simple formula describes many steps of rule 30 evolution
statement: Minimal Boolean formulas (in disjunctive normal form or in Nand operations) for the outcome of rule 30 grow rapidly with the number of steps, unlike those for simple rules such as 90 and 254, indicating that no simple formula describes rule 30 evolution and that, in most cases, cellular automaton patterns have no simple mathematical formula.
quote: So even if one allows rather general structure, the evidence is that in the end there is no way to set up any simple formula that will describe the outcome of evolution for a system like rule 30.
scope: formula representations of cellular automaton evolution, especially rule 30

label: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons
statement: Human memory likely retrieves data by a simple hashing-like mechanism in which successive layers of nerve cells, each responding to patterns in fixed random sets of inputs, produce representations that are the same for inputs differing by small changes, allowing retrieval by similarity.
quote: this basic mechanism provides a simple way to get a representation—and thus a hash code—that will tend to be the same for pieces of data that somehow have enough features that are similar.
scope: mechanisms of human memory storage and retrieval

label: Memory retrieval, not logic, underlies almost all of human thinking
statement: Retrieval from memory on the basis of similarity underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking, including generalization, analogy and intuition, and logical reasoning is not fundamental but is itself carried out by retrieving learned patterns of argument from memory.
quote: My strong suspicion is that the use of memory is what in fact underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking.
scope: human cognition

label: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules
statement: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.
quote: I strongly suspect that there is a definite core to the phenomenon of human thinking that is largely independent of such details—and that will in the end turn out to be based on rules that are rather simple.
scope: human thinking and its emulation by artificial systems

label: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions
statement: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.
quote: most likely it will at some level be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than to set up some special version of human-like thinking only for specific tasks.
scope: artificial intelligence and emulation of human thinking

label: Practical perception and analysis methods recognize only repetition and nesting
statement: Essentially all methods of perception and analysis in practical use have similar capabilities, recognizing repetition and sometimes nesting but almost nothing more complex, possibly because only such regularities are both common and quickly recognizable, or because humans choose methods matching their built-in perception.
quote: Most of them, for example, recognize repetition, and some also recognize nesting. But almost none recognize anything more complex.
scope: human perception and standard methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis

label: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities
statement: No method of perception and analysis, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize all possible regularities and thus tell immediately whether a piece of data can be generated from some simple description, although higher methods could recognize some regularities current methods miss.
quote: My strong belief—as I will argue in Chapter 12—is that at least in complete generality this will never be possible.
scope: all possible methods of perception and analysis

label: Extraterrestrial signals taken for noise could be meaningful messages
statement: Some extraterrestrial radio and other signals that are detected and assumed to be random noise could be meaningful messages encoded in a way recognizable only by higher forms of perception and analysis than those applied so far.
quote: it seems far from inconceivable that some of the extraterrestrial radio and other signals that we pick up and assume to be random noise could in fact be meaningful messages
scope: astronomical radio and other signals searched for extraterrestrial intelligence

label: Computation is the central organizing idea of the new science
statement: The most important idea underlying Wolfram's new kind of science is computation: systems such as cellular automata should be viewed as computations, with initial conditions as input and later states as output, so that systems with entirely different rules can be discussed in a unified, abstract way.
quote: And in many respects the single most important idea that underlies this new science is the notion of computation.
scope: the methodology of the new kind of science; cellular automata and other simple programs

label: Any system can be viewed as performing a computation
statement: Any system whatsoever, not just a cellular automaton, can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.
quote: At some level, any cellular automaton—or for that matter, any system whatsoever—can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.
scope: all systems, natural or artificial

label: Universality is crucial for understanding complexity in natural systems
statement: Although universality has never before been seriously considered in natural science, it is crucial for finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity seen in natural systems.
quote: But what I will show in this chapter and the next is that in fact universality is for example quite crucial in finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity we see in natural systems.
scope: natural systems exhibiting complex behavior

label: A universal system can produce arbitrarily complex behavior
statement: Because a universal system can emulate any other system, it can produce behavior as complex as that of any other system, so knowing a system is universal implies it can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
quote: So knowing that a particular system is universal thus immediately implies that the system can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
scope: universal computational systems of any kind

label: Universality is widespread and occurs in many systems in nature
statement: Contrary to the assumption that universality is rare and found only in systems specifically constructed to have it, universality is a widespread phenomenon that also occurs in a wide range of important systems found in nature.
quote: But one of the results of this chapter is that in fact universality is a much more widespread phenomenon. And in the next chapter I will argue that for example it also occurs in a wide range of important systems that we see in nature.
scope: computational and natural systems in general

label: A fixed universal cellular automaton can emulate any cellular automaton
statement: A single cellular automaton with fixed rules (Wolfram's 19-color, next-nearest-neighbor construction) can, given suitable initial conditions, emulate any cellular automaton whatsoever, regardless of how many colors or neighbors its rules involve, including rules more complicated than its own.
quote: And the conclusion is therefore that the universal cellular automaton can ultimately emulate a cellular automaton with absolutely any set of rules, regardless of how many neighbors and how many colors they may involve.
scope: one-dimensional cellular automata with any number of colors and any neighborhood size

label: Cellular automata can emulate nearly all other system types, even computers
statement: Cellular automata can be set up to emulate almost every type of system considered in the book—mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, sequential substitution and tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems, logic circuits and random-access memory—and in principle a practical computer in its entirety.
quote: But what I will show in this section is that in fact this is not the case, and that in the end cellular automata can actually be made to emulate almost every single type of system that we have discussed in this book.
scope: cellular automata versus mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems and practical computers

label: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step
statement: Unlike mobile automata or Turing machines, substitution systems cannot in general be emulated one step per cellular automaton step, because the number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor each step while a cellular automaton pattern can grow only by a fixed amount per step; progressively more cellular automaton steps are needed per substitution step.
quote: That this must ultimately be the case one can see from the fact that the total number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor from one step to the next, while in a cellular automaton the size of a pattern can only ever increase by a fixed amount at each step.
scope: cellular automaton emulation of substitution systems

label: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members
statement: Since a universal cellular automaton exists, any type of system shown capable of emulating any cellular automaton—including mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbor-dependent and sequential substitution systems, tag systems, cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines—must contain universal examples.
quote: And as soon as one knows that any particular type of system is capable of emulating any cellular automaton, it immediately follows that there must be examples of that type of system that are universal.
scope: mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems, register machines

label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata
statement: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only generate repetitive or nested patterns, so they cannot emulate cellular automata such as rule 30, whereas neighbor-dependent substitution systems can emulate cellular automata straightforwardly.
quote: For as we discussed on page 83, neighbor-independent substitution systems can generate only patterns that are either repetitive or nested—so they can never yield the more complicated patterns that are, for example, needed to emulate rule 30.
scope: neighbor-independent and neighbor-dependent substitution systems

label: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal
statement: A system that repeatedly takes a whole number, computes its remainder modulo a constant and applies an arithmetic operation chosen by that remainder can emulate a register machine, and is therefore universal; given how widespread universality is, arithmetic supporting it is unsurprising.
quote: The picture below shows that such a system can be set up to emulate a register machine. And from the fact that register machines are universal it follows that so too are such arithmetic systems.
scope: generalized arithmetic (Collatz-like) iteration systems

label: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent
statement: Because essentially all the kinds of systems studied (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and others) can emulate each other, a wide variety of systems with very different underlying structures are fundamentally equivalent in the computations they can perform, so computation can be studied abstractly with results applying across systems.
quote: In a sense its most important consequence is that it implies that from a computational point of view a very wide variety of systems, with very different underlying structures, are at some level fundamentally equivalent.
scope: cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and other simple programs

label: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability
statement: As systems of a given type are given progressively greater computational capabilities they eventually pass a threshold of universality, after which the set of computations they can perform is always the same, so more sophisticated rules gain nothing further and a universal system's capabilities are independent of the details of its construction.
quote: But the phenomenon of universality implies that this is not the case, and that as soon as one has passed the threshold of universality, nothing more can in a sense ever be gained.
scope: all universal systems, of any type

label: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110 is universal
statement: Rule 110, a two-color nearest-neighbor elementary cellular automaton, is universal: by arranging its naturally occurring localized structures as components, it can be made to emulate any cyclic tag system, and hence any Turing machine.
quote: And indeed in the case of rule 110 it took several years of work to develop the necessary ideas and tools. But finally it has turned out to be possible to show that the rule 110 cellular automaton is in fact universal.
scope: the rule 110 elementary cellular automaton

label: Universality should be common, including among very simple rules
statement: The universality of rule 110, one of the simplest possible cellular automaton rules, implies that universality is far more common than previously thought and should occur in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
quote: But knowing that a system like rule 110 is universal, the whole picture changes, and now it seems likely that instead universality should actually be seen in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
scope: simple programs of all kinds

label: Complexity of behavior saturates soon after the simplest rules
statement: As rules become progressively more complicated, overall behavior grows more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached, and since that threshold is very low, behavior beyond the very simplest rules of any kind should quickly become as complex as it will ever be—consistent with the Chapter 3 survey.
quote: So what this means is that if one looks at a sequence of systems with progressively more complicated rules, one should expect that the overall behavior they produce will become more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached.
scope: cellular automata, Turing machines and other simple programs enumerated by rule complexity

label: All class 4 cellular automata are expected to be universal
statement: Any cellular automaton showing class 4 behavior (localized structures moving and interacting in complicated ways) will, like rule 110, turn out to be universal, because such rules eventually yield localized structures rich enough to support universality.
quote: I strongly suspect that it is true in general that any cellular automaton which shows overall class 4 behavior will turn out—like rule 110—to be universal.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Rule 110 and its reflections are the only clear elementary class 4 rules
statement: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, the only clear immediate example of class 4 behavior is rule 110 together with its left-right and black-white equivalents (rules 124, 137 and 193), while class 4 behavior is common once more colors or neighbors are allowed, even for totalistic rules.
quote: Among the 256 so-called elementary cellular automata that allow only two possible colors for each cell and depend only on nearest neighbors, the only clear immediate example is rule 110—together with rules 124, 137 and 193 obtained by trivially reversing left and right or black and white.
scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata and multi-color or larger-neighborhood rules

label: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal
statement: Cellular automata that produce only uniform or repetitive patterns (class 1 and class 2) can never be universal, because they transmit information only over limited distances and so support only processes involving a limited number of cells.
quote: In a sense the fundamental reason for this—as we discussed on page 252—is that such class 1 and class 2 cellular automata never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances.
scope: class 1 and class 2 cellular automata

label: Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal
statement: Cellular automata whose information transmission is highly constrained so that patterns are essentially nested, and additive rules such as rules 90 and 150 whose states after a power-of-two number of steps are simple superpositions of shifted copies of the initial condition, cannot be universal.
quote: And since there are many kinds of behavior that do not return to such predictable forms after any limited number of steps, one must conclude that additive rules cannot be universal.
scope: additive and nested-pattern cellular automata, e.g. rules 90 and 150

label: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions
statement: Rule 54, a possible class 4 elementary cellular automaton, shows only repetitive or nested behavior in its first hundred million initial conditions, leaving it uncertain whether rule 54 is universal.
quote: And as one continues one sees various other repetitive and nested forms. But at least up to the hundred millionth initial condition one sees nothing that is fundamentally any more complicated.
scope: the rule 54 elementary cellular automaton

label: Any non-repetitive, non-nested system is expected to be universal
statement: More or less any system whose behavior is not fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal, so there is a close connection between universality and the appearance of complex behavior, though proving it will be far easier for some systems (such as rule 110) than others.
quote: As I will discuss in the next chapter, my general expectation is that more or less any system whose behavior is not somehow fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal.
scope: all systems showing complex (non-repetitive, non-nested) behavior

label: Uncontrolled information flow in class 3 rules hinders universality proofs
statement: Universality proofs proceed by building components from localized structures, which requires controlled transmission of information; in class 3 systems a change to a single cell eventually spreads to all cells, making it very hard to identify definite components and hence to prove universality.
quote: And this kind of uncontrolled transmission of information makes it very difficult to identify pieces that could be used as definite components in a construction.
scope: class 3 cellular automata and methods for proving universality

label: Rules 30 and 45 are expected to be universal
statement: Although the localized structures found in rules 30 and 45 on repetitive backgrounds all move at the same speed and so cannot interact, preventing a rule 110-style proof, rules 30 and 45 will nevertheless turn out to be universal.
quote: So although this means that the particular type of approach we used to demonstrate the universality of rule 110 cannot immediately be used for rule 30 or rule 45, it certainly does not mean that these rules are not in the end universal.
scope: the rule 30 and rule 45 elementary cellular automata

label: Complex elementary rules can emulate one step of every elementary rule
statement: Using block encodings, elementary rules with complex behavior such as rules 22, 30 and 110 can be made to emulate a single step of all 256 elementary cellular automata, whereas rules with simple behavior such as 90 and 184 can emulate only a few; this supports the idea that complex-looking cellular automata can do arbitrarily sophisticated computations.
quote: But for underlying rules that have more complex behavior—like rules 22, 30, or 110—it turns out that in the end it is always possible to emulate all 256 elementary rules.
scope: single-step block emulation among the 256 elementary cellular automata

label: Perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal
statement: Since elementary cellular automata whose behavior looks complex can do computations as sophisticated as desired, they are expected to be universal, so perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal.
quote: And this suggests that such cellular automata will in the end turn out to be universal—with the result that out of the 256 elementary rules one expects that perhaps as many as 27 will in fact be universal.
scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata

label: A 2-state 5-color Turing machine is universal via rule 110
statement: A Turing machine with just 2 states and 5 colors, far simpler than the 7-state 4-color machine that had long been the simplest known, is universal because it emulates rule 110 by sweeping back and forth and updating all cells by one rule 110 step per sweep.
quote: And in fact, by using the universality of rule 110 it turns out to be possible to come up with the vastly simpler universal Turing machine shown below—with just 2 states and 5 possible colors.
scope: small universal Turing machines

label: No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal
statement: All 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors have behavior too simple to support universality.
quote: If one looks at the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors it is fairly easy to see that their behavior is in all cases too simple to support universality.
scope: 2-state 2-color Turing machines

label: Complex behavior is rare but present in small Turing machine spaces
statement: Starting from a blank tape, roughly one in 50,000 2-state 4-color Turing machines and one in 200,000 4-state 2-color machines show complex behavior, and 14 essentially equivalent machines among the 2,985,984 with 2 states and 3 colors do so.
quote: Among such 2-state 4-color Turing machines perhaps one in 50,000 shows complex behavior when started from a blank tape.
scope: 2-state 4-color, 4-state 2-color and 2-state 3-color Turing machines

label: A complex 2-state 3-color Turing machine is likely the simplest universal one
statement: The 2-state 3-color Turing machine numbered 596,440, which yields complicated behavior from a blank tape, is likely universal, and if so would by most measures be the simplest universal Turing machine.
quote: And although it will no doubt be very difficult to prove, it seems likely that this Turing machine will in the end turn out to be universal. And if so, then presumably it will by most measures be the very simplest Turing machine that is universal.
scope: 2-state 3-color Turing machines

label: All 3-state 2-color Turing machines behave simply from blank tape
statement: With blank initial conditions all 2,985,984 Turing machines with 3 states and 2 colors quickly produce simple repetitive or nested behavior, and even with more complicated initial conditions their behavior eventually seems to resolve into a simple form.
quote: With 3 states and 2 colors it turns out that with blank initial conditions all of the 2,985,984 possible Turing machines of this type quickly evolve to produce simple repetitive or nested behavior.
scope: 3-state 2-color Turing machines

label: Combinators show highly complex behavior despite simple rules
statement: Combinators, symbolic systems long known to be universal, show highly complex behavior despite simple rules—for example a length-8 initial expression grows exponentially with seemingly random internal structure—and they can emulate rule 110, suggesting their universality is just associated with general complex behavior.
quote: But from pictures like the ones on the facing page it is rather clear that despite their fairly simple underlying rules, the behavior of combinators can be highly complex.
scope: S and K combinator systems

label: Every process, natural or artificial, can be viewed as a computation
statement: Any process that follows definite rules, including processes in nature governed by physical law as well as processes constructed by humans, can be viewed as a computation, giving a uniform framework for comparing very different processes.
quote: all processes, whether they are produced by human effort or occur spontaneously in nature, can be viewed as computations.
scope: all natural and artificial processes

label: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication
statement: Almost all processes whose behavior is not obviously simple correspond to computations of equivalent sophistication; there is essentially a single highest level of computational sophistication, and almost all such processes reach it regardless of how simple their rules or initial conditions are.
quote: the most general is just to say that almost all processes that are not obviously simple can be viewed as computations of equivalent sophistication.
scope: essentially all processes in nature, mathematics and engineered systems whose behavior is not obviously simple

label: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal
statement: Among all possible rules of a given type (such as cellular automata) whose behavior is not obviously simple, i.e. not repetitive or nested, the overwhelming majority are computationally universal, so universality is extremely common rather than a rare engineered property.
quote: among all possible systems with behavior that is not obviously simple an overwhelming fraction are universal.
scope: enumerable classes of simple programs such as cellular automata, Turing machines and related systems

label: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines
statement: As a law of nature, no system that can actually be constructed in our universe can carry out explicit computations more sophisticated than those of universal systems such as cellular automata and Turing machines; imaginable hypercomputers (e.g. with infinite tables of results) cannot be built.
quote: no system can ever carry out explicit computations that are more sophisticated than those carried out by systems like cellular automata and Turing machines.
scope: all physical systems in our universe, including computers and brains

label: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected
statement: When no constraint such as engineering design or natural selection forces simple behavior, the rules that operate in nature are effectively selected in no special way apart from tending to be structurally simple, so they behave like randomly chosen rules and are almost always universal when their behavior is not obviously simple.
quote: most rules that appear in nature can be viewed as being selected in no special way—save perhaps for the fact that the structure of the rules themselves tends to be fairly simple.
scope: rules governing natural systems not constrained by engineering or natural selection

label: Rule 30 from a single cell contains every possible block
statement: The pattern generated by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell appears to contain every possible block of cells eventually, so that essentially any possible computation exists somewhere within this single pattern.
quote: So far as I can tell, all possible blocks eventually appear, potentially letting the pattern serve as a kind of directory of all possible computations.
scope: rule 30 elementary cellular automaton started from a single black cell

label: Continuous systems cannot exceed discrete computation in practice
statement: Continuous systems, including analog computers, systems described by continuous equations, and even idealized perfectly continuous systems under reasonable assumptions, cannot perform computations fundamentally more sophisticated than discrete systems like cellular automata; continuity is largely an idealization.
quote: even idealized perfectly continuous systems will never in fact be able to perform fundamentally more sophisticated computations.
scope: analog computers, continuous mathematical models, and physical systems treated as continuous

label: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations
statement: Whereas solving pure polynomial equations allows no computation beyond that of ordinary discrete systems, once trigonometric functions are allowed one can construct equations whose solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of infinitely many steps of a system like a cellular automaton.
quote: as soon as one even allows trigonometric functions, for example, it turns out that it becomes possible to construct equations for which finding a solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of an infinite number of steps in the evolution of a system like a cellular automaton.
scope: equations built from standard mathematical functions

label: Complicated molecules generally do not reach minimum-energy configurations
statement: Although simple molecules may settle into minimum-energy configurations, complicated molecules typically do not; they explore configurations by an explicit evolution process, so nature does not actually solve hard constraint-satisfaction problems as traditional models idealize.
quote: while in simple cases complicated molecules may for example arrange themselves in configurations that minimize energy, the evidence is that in more complicated cases they typically do not.
scope: molecular configurations such as large biomolecules and glasses

label: Human thinking rests on rather simple computational processes
statement: The basic mechanisms of human thinking will turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes, so human thought does not perform computations beyond the level allowed by the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
quote: the basic mechanisms of human thinking will in the end turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes.
scope: human brains and thinking

label: No hidden regularity beyond repetition and nesting in rule-30-like systems
statement: There is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems with complex behavior such as rule 30; beyond systems with obvious regularities like repetition and nesting, most systems are universal and computationally equivalent.
quote: I have gradually come to the conclusion that there is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems, and that instead what the Principle of Computational Equivalence suggests is correct
scope: simple programs with non-repetitive, non-nested behavior, such as rule 30

label: Complexity arises because observers are computationally equivalent to systems
statement: Systems with simple rules appear complex because, once a low threshold is passed, their evolution is as computationally sophisticated as any process of perception or analysis used to study them, and this holds for any method of perception and analysis that can actually be used.
quote: observers will tend to be computationally equivalent to the systems they observe—with the inevitable consequence that they will consider the behavior of such systems complex.
scope: observers (human or otherwise) studying systems in nature and simple programs

label: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior
statement: For computationally irreducible systems, even with complete knowledge of rules and initial conditions, there is no way to predict the behavior except by performing almost as many computational steps as the system's own evolution.
quote: there can be no way to predict how the system will behave except by going through almost as many steps of computation as the evolution of the system itself.
scope: any system whose evolution is computationally irreducible

label: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible
statement: Behavior that is obviously simple, such as repetitive or nested behavior, is always computationally reducible, while in practically all other cases behavior is computationally irreducible.
quote: If the behavior of a system is obviously simple—and is say either repetitive or nested—then it will always be computationally reducible. But it follows from the Principle of Computational Equivalence that in practically all other cases it will be computationally irreducible.
scope: all systems, especially simple programs
